originalGroup.material:
A. Planning a book sale

The four emails below use the same local time.

From: Nina
To: Sam; Iris
Sent: 10 November 2026, 09:00
Subject: A date for the book sale

Hi both, we need to choose between 21 and 28 November for our second-hand book sale. I can help on either date, but I must leave at noon. The community room is available on both days. We will need time to put the books on tables before visitors arrive. Which date works for you?

From: Sam
To: Nina; Iris
Sent: 10 November 2026, 09:12
Subject: Re: A date for the book sale

I am away on 21 November. On the 28th, I can arrive at 10:30 and stay until the room closes at 13:00. I cannot carry the boxes from the store before then, but I can help at a sales table and put things away afterwards.

From: Iris
To: Nina; Sam
Sent: 10 November 2026, 10:05
Subject: Re: A date for the book sale

The 28th is good for me. I have the key to the room and can get there at 09:30. My brother has offered to help us carry the boxes at that time. We should finish selling early enough to clean the room before it closes.

From: Nina
To: Sam; Iris
Sent: 10 November 2026, 11:20
Subject: Final plan

Let's choose 28 November. Iris, please bring the key at 09:30. I will meet you and your brother to set up. Sam can join us at 10:30. We will open the sale at 11:00 and finish selling at 12:30. I will leave at noon, so Sam and Iris will need to handle the last half hour and the cleaning. Thanks, everyone!

B. Testing a paper bridge

In a fictional classroom project, a science club compared two paper-bridge designs. One used a flat sheet; the other used a sheet folded into four long ridges. The students wanted to know which design could hold more identical metal counters before falling between two supports.

They cut every sheet to the same size and kept the supports ten centimetres apart. Counters were added one at a time at the centre of each bridge. Every trial used a fresh sheet, so a bridge weakened by an earlier test was never used again.

The flat bridges held 4, 5, 5, 6 and 5 counters. The folded bridges held 12, 14, 15, 13 and 16. The average was therefore 5 counters for the flat design and 14 for the folded design. The students recorded every trial, including the ones that held fewer counters than expected.

One member wanted the report to say that folding paper always made it stronger. The group decided that this would go beyond their test. They had compared one kind of paper, one folding pattern and one distance between supports. They had not compared every possible fold or tested whether the bridges behaved the same way over a wider gap.

Their final report described the folded design as the better performer in this particular comparison. For a follow-up project, they planned to keep the paper and the distance unchanged while trying a different folding pattern. The question would become more specific, not less useful: which features of the fold appeared to matter under the same test conditions?

questions.material:
B. Testing a paper bridge

In a fictional classroom project, a science club compared two paper-bridge designs. One used a flat sheet; the other used a sheet folded into four long ridges. The students wanted to know which design could hold more identical metal counters before falling between two supports.

They cut every sheet to the same size and kept the supports ten centimetres apart. Counters were added one at a time at the centre of each bridge. Every trial used a fresh sheet, so a bridge weakened by an earlier test was never used again.

The flat bridges held 4, 5, 5, 6 and 5 counters. The folded bridges held 12, 14, 15, 13 and 16. The average was therefore 5 counters for the flat design and 14 for the folded design. The students recorded every trial, including the ones that held fewer counters than expected.

One member wanted the report to say that folding paper always made it stronger. The group decided that this would go beyond their test. They had compared one kind of paper, one folding pattern and one distance between supports. They had not compared every possible fold or tested whether the bridges behaved the same way over a wider gap.

Their final report described the folded design as the better performer in this particular comparison. For a follow-up project, they planned to keep the paper and the distance unchanged while trying a different folding pattern. The question would become more specific, not less useful: which features of the fold appeared to matter under the same test conditions?

Whether the supports were made of metal or wood.
Whether counters were placed in the centre or on the edges.

originalGroup.material:
A. Arranging a recorded interview

All four emails use the same local date and time zone.

From: Eli
To: May; Jorge
Sent: 12 November 2026, 10:00
Subject: Our local-history interview

Ms Reed has agreed to speak to us on 21 November for our school project. We need a quiet room for a half-hour interview. May, could we use the community room? Jorge, when could you arrive to help with the recorder?

From: May
To: Eli; Jorge
Sent: 12 November 2026, 10:20
Subject: Re: Our local-history interview

The room is available until noon, but there will be a piano rehearsal next door from 10:00 to 11:00. It will be much quieter afterwards. I can bring copies of the old street photographs that Ms Reed has offered to discuss.

From: Jorge
To: Eli; May
Sent: 12 November 2026, 11:05
Subject: Re: Our local-history interview

My class finishes at 10:40, and it takes me ten minutes to walk to the community room. I can test the recorder before the interview. Please check whether Ms Reed is happy for us to record both sound and video.

From: Eli
To: May; Jorge
Sent: 12 November 2026, 12:10
Subject: Confirmed arrangements

Ms Reed is happy for us to record her voice, but she does not want to appear in a video. Her bus arrives at 11:10 and she needs five minutes to walk to the room, so let's start at 11:15 and finish at 11:45. Jorge, please test the recorder at 10:55. May and I will arrange the chairs and photographs. We must leave the room before noon.

B. The voice behind the school radio

For her first school-radio programme, Hana wanted a guest whose name everyone would recognise. When the sports captain was unavailable, her teacher suggested interviewing Mr Cole, who opened the school building each morning. Hana was polite, but privately wondered whether the conversation would interest anyone.

She prepared questions about keys, lights and early buses. Mr Cole answered them, then mentioned that he once repaired stage equipment for a travelling theatre group. He had worked behind curtains while actors performed in small halls across the country. Hana stopped looking at her list and asked him about the first performance he remembered.

The interview produced more material than the eight-minute programme could contain. Hana's first edit kept the fastest stories and removed most of the pauses. When she listened again, the conversation sounded rushed. In one place, Mr Cole's answer seemed to disagree with a question that had actually come later in the original recording.

Hana returned to the complete recording. She chose fewer stories, kept each question with its answer and left short pauses where Mr Cole had been thinking. Before broadcasting, she played the edited version to him and checked that she had represented his meaning accurately.

The programme did not turn Mr Cole into a celebrity. It did make several students stop to talk to him about theatre. Hana learned that finding an interesting story was not always a matter of finding the most famous person. It could begin with taking an ordinary meeting seriously—and continue with enough care not to lose someone's meaning while making it fit the time available.

questions.prompt: How did Hana initially feel about interviewing Mr Cole?
questions.material:
B. The voice behind the school radio

For her first school-radio programme, Hana wanted a guest whose name everyone would recognise. When the sports captain was unavailable, her teacher suggested interviewing Mr Cole, who opened the school building each morning. Hana was polite, but privately wondered whether the conversation would interest anyone.

She prepared questions about keys, lights and early buses. Mr Cole answered them, then mentioned that he once repaired stage equipment for a travelling theatre group. He had worked behind curtains while actors performed in small halls across the country. Hana stopped looking at her list and asked him about the first performance he remembered.

The interview produced more material than the eight-minute programme could contain. Hana's first edit kept the fastest stories and removed most of the pauses. When she listened again, the conversation sounded rushed. In one place, Mr Cole's answer seemed to disagree with a question that had actually come later in the original recording.

Hana returned to the complete recording. She chose fewer stories, kept each question with its answer and left short pauses where Mr Cole had been thinking. Before broadcasting, she played the edited version to him and checked that she had represented his meaning accurately.

The programme did not turn Mr Cole into a celebrity. It did make several students stop to talk to him about theatre. Hana learned that finding an interesting story was not always a matter of finding the most famous person. It could begin with taking an ordinary meeting seriously—and continue with enough care not to lose someone's meaning while making it fit the time available.

options.text: She doubted whether he would have an interesting story.
She already knew all about his theatre experience.
She wanted him to replace the sports captain on the school team.
